subject: typescript
title: Interfaces
description: Describing object shapes, optional and readonly members, extends, and interface vs type.

content.title: Definition
content.body: An interface describes the shape of an object: which properties exist and what type each one holds. It is a compile-time contract only — no code is generated for it.

content.title: Optional and readonly
content.body: A ? marks a property that may be absent; readonly blocks reassignment after construction.

content.title: Good practice
content.body: Reach for an interface for object shapes you extend, and a type alias for unions, tuples and mapped types. Interfaces also merge across declarations, which is useful for augmenting library types and surprising everywhere else.

exercises.question: Which TypeScript construct describes the shape of an object and can be extended?
exercises.explanation: An interface describes an object shape and supports extends; type aliases use intersections instead.

exercises.question: What is the type of u.email inside the function?
exercises.explanation: A ? adds undefined to the property's type. Read it behind a check, or the strict compiler will complain downstream.

exercises.question: Which line does the compiler reject?

answers.text: Line 1 — an interface cannot hold two members of the same type
Line 4 — objects cannot be logged directly
Line 3 — z is an excess property on an object literal

exercises.explanation: Object literals assigned straight to an annotated target get an excess-property check. Assigning through a variable first would pass, since structural typing only requires the members to be present.

exercises.question: Complete the declaration so Admin has every User member plus one of its own.
exercises.explanation: Interfaces inherit with extends. implements is for classes; & is the intersection operator used with type aliases.

exercises.question: Marking a property readonly also prevents mutating the object stored in it.
exercises.explanation: readonly is shallow: you cannot reassign the property, but you can still push into a readonly array property or edit a nested object.

exercises.question: An object with extra properties is stored in a variable and then passed to a function expecting Point. What happens?

answers.text: It is rejected, because the shapes are not identical
It is accepted, but the extra properties are deleted
It only works if Point is a class
It is accepted — TypeScript only requires the expected members to be present

exercises.explanation: TypeScript is structurally typed: compatibility is about the members required, not about names or declaration sites.

exercises.question: Complete the index signature for a string-keyed lookup of numbers.
exercises.explanation: Index signature keys may be string, number or symbol. Record<string, number> expresses the same thing more compactly.

exercises.question: TypeScript · interfaces
exercises.front: Two interfaces with the same name
exercises.back: Merge into one — their members are combined rather than clashing
exercises.explanation: Only interfaces do this. Declaring the same type alias twice is an error, which is often what you actually want.

exercises.question: Which call satisfies this interface?

answers.text: repo.find("u1") — returning a plain string synchronously
await repo.find("u1") — returning a string or null

exercises.explanation: The signature requires one string argument and returns a promise, so the call site awaits it and handles null.

exercises.question: Which statement is true of a type alias but not of an interface?

answers.text: It can describe a union, a tuple or a mapped type
It can describe an object shape
It can be implemented by a class

exercises.explanation: Interfaces only describe object-like shapes. Aliases cover everything, but do not merge across declarations — which is usually an advantage.

exercises.question: Under exactOptionalPropertyTypes, which assignment is rejected?

answers.text: b — an explicitly undefined value is not the same as an absent property

exercises.explanation: The flag separates "not provided" from "provided as undefined", which matters for anything that spreads or merges options objects.

exercises.question: Complete the class declaration so the compiler checks it against the interface.
exercises.explanation: implements checks the shape without inheriting anything. extends is for inheriting from a base class.

exercises.question: A function typed (a: string) => void is assignable to a property typed (a: string, b: number) => void.
exercises.explanation: Ignoring trailing parameters is always safe. It is why array callbacks can take just the element and skip the index.

exercises.question: Which line does the compiler reject?

answers.text: Line 3 — push mutates a readonly property
Line 4 — the property cannot be reassigned
Line 2 — the array literal is not readonly
Line 1 — readonly cannot be used on an array

exercises.explanation: readonly is shallow: it blocks reassignment, not mutation. readonly string[] would have rejected line 3 as well.

exercises.question: Why add a literal `kind` field to each member of a union of interfaces?

answers.text: It lets a switch narrow the union, and makes an unhandled member a compile error
It is required for interfaces to be unioned

exercises.explanation: Without a discriminant the compiler can only offer members every branch shares, and adding a new case fails silently at every call site.
